title: Redwood POC Weekly Sync - Quantaco AI (cost review)
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on unit economics. Reviewed tokens/sec/$ metrics from last week's benchmark, discussed KV/prefix caching savings, and batching tradeoffs. Agreed on next benchmarks for 512/2k contexts and action items for cost-optimized config and permissioning for Dedicated trial.
next_steps: Redwood to share detailed cost spreadsheet and model-by-model token throughput table (Ethan)
Quantaco to run a 2k-context benchmark with prefix caching enabled and report hit rate (Lina)
Schedule security handoff for Dedicated trial (Maya + Tomás) - week of 7/21
Align on success criteria for POC (Ravi + Maya)
action_items: Ethan Morales: export tokens/sec/$ table and send spreadsheet by 2025-07-18
Lina Park: run 2k-context run with prefix caching and share logs by 2025-07-23
Maya Chen: set up Dedicated trial access request, include KMS notes by 2025-07-20
Tomás Vega: provide internal firewall/VPC details for onboarding by 2025-07-22
meeting_header:
Date: 2025-07-16
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen, Ethan Morales, Priya Nair (Redwood) — Ravi Kumar, Lina Park, Tomás Vega, Asha Mehta (Quantaco AI)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick check in, we're focusing on the cost/unit economics part of the POC today, tokens per second per dollar, caching and batching tradeoffs.
[00:12] Ravi Kumar: Yup thanks Maya, we've been looking at last week's numbers, wanted to walk through some of the outliers, we saw variable hit rates on caching and that changed our cost estimates.
[00:25] Ethan Morales: Cool, I have the spreadsheet open. Quick reminder — our metric tokens/sec/$ is basically normalized throughput divided by the per-hour cost of the instance. It's start simple. For example, on A100-type profiles we see about 1,800 tokens/sec on a single worker for the smaller 2B-ish model, cost comes in at roughly $X/hour in the sandbox — which converts to about 900 tokens/sec per dollar in that run. OK those numbers are rough, we put exacts in the sheet.
[01:02] Lina Park: Real question — what's our baseline for typical request size? Our production median is ~420 tokens (prompt + response) and 95th is ~2k. That 2k tail is the one blowing up the per-request cost for us.
[01:18] Priya Nair: Right, and the caching piece helps mainly for repeated prefixes — we saw about a 30% cost reduction when prefix cache hit rate was 40 to 50% in the last test. If you can push hit rates above 60% you start to see diminishing returns but still meaningful savings.
[01:40] Tomás Vega: Our concern from infra side is latency — batching helps amortize cost but adds 60 to 120 ms of queuing depending on arrival patterns. We need sub-200ms p95 for interactive features.
[01:55] Ethan Morales: Totally. So tradeoff is: larger batch => more tokens/sec/$ because GPU amortization improves, but p95 latency increases. We recommend an adaptive batcher with low-latency bin for priority traffic and high-throughput bin for background jobs. That gets you best of both worlds.
[02:20] Asha Mehta: Can you quantify the tokens/sec/$ improvement with batching?
[02:25] Ethan Morales: On our tests, moving from batch size 1 to 8 improved tokens/sec/$ by ~2.7x on the smaller models, and ~1.9x on the large 13B family. Those are under steady-state synthetic load. Real-world with variable seq length you'll see less; the spreadsheet has per-model numbers.
[02:52] Ravi Kumar: About caching — prefix vs KV cache, what's the difference in practice for us?
[02:58] Maya Chen: Prefix caching is essentially full token prefix reuse — good when users repeat prompts or templates. KV cache is the internal transformer key-value cache reuse within a session; it's automatically leveraged for multi-turn chat to avoid recomputing early layers. For Quantaco's use-case, we saw large gains from prefix caching because you have repeated boilerplate instructions across many calls.
[03:20] Lina Park: We ran an experiment where we enabled prefix cache for the legal-template flow and hit rate was only 38% because prompts had small personalization tokens. How do we get more hit rate?
[03:32] Priya Nair: You can normalize personalization — extract user-specific slots and pass them as metadata so the prefix becomes stable. We can share tooling for prompt templating — that gave the customer in our other pilot about +20% hit rate improvement.
[03:45] Tomás Vega: Is there any security or privacy issue with prefix caching if prompts contain PII?
[03:49] Maya Chen: Good callout. If using Hosted, we offer configurable retention and redaction options. For Dedicated/Private you control data at rest and KMS. We'll include the specific SSO/KMS notes in the security packet.
[04:03] Ethan Morales: Back to numbers — last week's run on your sample workload (420 median tokens) showed per-call cost of ~ $0.0017 and tokens/sec/$ around 1200 for the 3B test instance when batching and caching were enabled. With caching off and batch=1 that dropped to ~380 tokens/sec/$ so you can see a 3x swing.
[04:32] Ravi Kumar: That matches the surprise we had. Our unit cost projections used batch=1 and caching off, which is why the POC looked expensive.
[04:40] Maya Chen: Exactly, for production we expect you to use both caching and batching. The question is how much latency budget you have per route. For interactive, keep low batch and the adaptive suggestion; for async indexing use max batching.
[04:55] Lina Park: For the 2k long tail requests, is context window size impacting tokens/sec/$ significantly?
[05:00] Ethan Morales: Yes — sequence length drives compute linearly for autoregressive models. For context window 2k vs 512, throughput drops roughly 3-4x depending on model. But if you can cache early tokens (prefix) and only slide KV for the delta, the effective cost is closer to the delta length. Hence caching is more valuable for long contexts.
[05:28] Tomás Vega: Any recommendations for quantization? We have some tolerance for slight quality drop.
[05:33] Priya Nair: Quantization to int8/4 (we recommend Redwood-verified quant profiles) reduces memory and increases tokens/sec on some hardware; cost improvements vary by model and hardware but we've seen 20-40% cost reduction with acceptable quality for retrieval-augmented flows. We'll include recommended quant profiles per model in the sheet.
[05:55] Asha Mehta: Competitors have been pitching "cheaper per token" using distillation and smaller models — how do you compare?
[06:02] Maya Chen: Distillation is valid if your accuracy needs allow. Our value prop here is providing consistent operational tooling so you can optimize cost (batching, caching, quant) and measure impact. For many customers the fastest path was a smaller distilled model for low latency and Redwood Optimize suggestions to tune throughput.
[06:20] Ravi Kumar: Okay, practical next step — we want Redwood to re-run a 2k-context benchmark with our real prompt set and enable prefix caching normalization. Lina will run from our side too, but it'd be useful for you to run a controlled run so we can compare.
[06:34] Ethan Morales: We'll schedule a controlled benchmark next week on a Dedicated worker and share the token-level traces. We'll also break out tokens/sec/$ across cold vs warm (cache hit/miss) and show where the wins are.
[06:46] Lina Park: From infra — for Dedicated what's the onboarding friction? We need VPC peering, KMS integration and audit logs.
[06:54] Maya Chen: We have a Dedicated onboarding checklist. It includes VPC peering steps, SAML/SSO, and KMS/HSM notes. We'll send the checklist and schedule a security handoff with Tomás.
[07:05] Tomás Vega: We'll share firewall and subnets, but need to understand egress and outbound controls — do you require open outbound?
[07:13] Maya Chen: No, Dedicated agent can work with restricted egress if you provide the required endpoints. We'll detail that in the security packet.
[07:21] Ravi Kumar: One more on billing model — if we commit to reserved Dedicated capacity, how does that change tokens/sec/$?
[07:28] Priya Nair: Reserved capacity drops hourly $ cost significantly; in our modeling a 30% reserved commit reduced per-token unit cost by roughly 25% depending on utilization. We'll include a sample committed vs on-demand curve in the spreadsheet.
[07:45] Ethan Morales: Quick note on benchmarking methodology: we'll report median throughput, p95 latency, and tokens/sec/$, and we'll include cache hit rate buckets (0-20, 20-40, 40-60, 60+). That way you can map where you'll land based on observed hit rates.
[08:02] Lina Park: Sounds good. Also can you annotate the spreadsheet with the assumptions (e.g., OS, GPU type, model quantization, batch settings)?
[08:08] Ethan Morales: Absolutely, all assumptions will be columned.
[08:12] Ravi Kumar: Any blockers for the 2k benchmark? We need Redwood to have access to the prompt corpus and for us to schedule a slot on your Dedicated pool.
[08:20] Maya Chen: We need a short data sharing agreement for the prompt set (we'll redact if needed), and we'll reserve a run slot — I'll coordinate offline.
[08:29] Tomás Vega: I'll work with Maya on security bits.
[08:33] Maya Chen: Great. To recap — Ethan will send the detailed cost tokens/sec/$ sheet by Friday (7/18), Redwood to schedule a Dedicated benchmark run for next week, Lina will run a mirror test and share cache hit logs, Tomás and Maya to schedule security handoff. Any objections?
[08:50] Ravi Kumar: No objections. This is helpful.
[08:54] Asha Mehta: Thanks, team.
[08:56] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email with links to the sheet and the onboarding checklist.
[09:02] END
notes: Transcript contains minor ASR errors and some speaker mislabels. Numbers labeled X in casual speech replaced with sheet values in follow-up email.
